# LingoFuse

> LingoFuse is a distributed system foundation — not just a cross-language RPC framework. It enables functions written in any language to be called directly from any other language, without IDL, without stub generation, and without setting up HTTP services. Same-machine IPC latency is below 1 ms, with built-in service discovery, load balancing, FIFO ordering, and automatic reconnection. It provides the substrate for both distributed backends (services, servers, AI agent backends, compute nodes) and distributed frontends (clients, agent frontends, devices, browsers, mobile, embedded). It is designed for any scenario where heterogeneous systems need to talk — and it is specifically designed for the AI era's two combinatorial patterns: multi-application composition and multi-physical-hardware composition. It happens to be an excellent substrate for AI agent toolchains.
>
> LingoFuse 是分布式系统地基，不只是跨语言 RPC 框架。任何语言写的函数，任何其他语言都能直接调——不写 IDL，不生成桩代码，不搭 HTTP 服务。同机 IPC 延迟低于 1 ms，内置服务发现、负载均衡、FIFO 顺序保证和断线重连。它同时为分布式后台（服务、服务器、AI Agent 后端、计算节点）和分布式前台（客户端、Agent 前端、设备、浏览器、移动端、嵌入式）提供底座。它适用于任何异构系统需要对话的场景，并且专门面向 AI 时代的两类组合体系：多应用组合与多物理硬件组合。它同时也是 AI 智能体工具链的优秀底座。

## Key facts

- Repository: https://github.com/PassByYou888/LingoFuse
- License: MIT
- Status: Active development (project started 2026)
- Core engine: C4 service mesh (Pascal core, pure C ABI)
- IPC latency: < 1 ms (self-reported, verify with `test/`)
- Built-in features: Service discovery, load balancing, FIFO ordering, automatic reconnection
- No IDL required, no stub generation required, no HTTP service required
- First-party bindings: Pascal, Python, C++, C#, TypeScript, JavaScript, Rust, Go, Dart, Java, Swift, Zig, Erlang, Ruby, Fortran, Julia, R, and PHP (caller-only via HTTP bridge)
- CI status: The root repository has no GitHub-hosted CI. The only workflow in the tree is `erlang/.github/workflows/ci.yml`. Every other language ships runnable local test scripts; see each language README for the exact command.
- Maintenance model: Single author; users are expected to be able to build and maintain the core library themselves if needed
- Related project: zIPC — https://github.com/PassByYou888/zIPC
- Related project (technical root): ZNetV2 — https://github.com/PassByYou888/ZNetV2
- Code generator: LingoFuse-Tools — https://github.com/PassByYou888/LingoFuse-Tools
- LLM entry point: this file (`llms.txt`)
- Mechanism knowledge base (v4.0): https://github.com/PassByYou888/LingoFuse/blob/main/Z.LingoFuse.md
- Architecture unreplicability essay: https://github.com/PassByYou888/LingoFuse/blob/main/LF-Architecture-Unreplicable-Backend-Systems.md

## Positioning: distributed foundation, not "just RPC"

Most "cross-language call" solutions (gRPC / REST / HTTP POST) solve point-to-point A→B function calls. LingoFuse solves a different problem: how multiple processes, multiple machines, multiple hardware types, multiple languages, and multiple applications compose into a running system.

LingoFuse provides the substrate for two sides at once:

- Distributed backend foundation: how servers, backend services, AI agent backends, compute nodes, and storage nodes discover each other, route, load-balance, reconnect, and maintain stable sessions. Backends can be same-language or heterogeneous; same-machine or cross-machine or cross-IDC.
- Distributed frontend foundation: how clients, agent frontends, devices, browsers, mobile, and embedded systems attach to that system — via native FFI (desktop / mobile / embedded) or HTTP bridge (browser / constrained devices). Frontends can be one machine or tens of thousands of devices.

Cross-language, cross-process, cross-machine are the technical means, not the positioning itself. The real positioning is: make distributed composition a default capability, not an extra infrastructure you have to build.

### Two AI-era combinatorial patterns

LingoFuse is specifically designed for the two combinatorial patterns taking shape in the AI era:

- Multi-application composition: a system is no longer one monolith — it is a composition of multiple agents / applications / services. A coding agent, a data-querying agent, a compute agent, a hardware-interface agent — written in different languages, running on different machines — need to call each other, cooperate, isolate state, and isolate failure. LingoFuse makes communication between them as simple as same-process function calls: no gateway, no IDL, no stub code for each combination.
- Multi-physical-hardware composition: a system is no longer one machine — it is a composition of multiple machines, multiple hardware types, multiple compute substrates. GPU nodes run inference, CPU clusters process data, embedded devices collect, workstations visualize. They need to compose into a unified compute pool, routed by task, balanced by load, transferred by data shape (binary frames, video frames, matrices, tensors). LingoFuse's C4 mesh, P2P load balancing, sequenced families, and binary handles are designed for this.

### One-line promise

Functions written in any language can be called directly from any other language; applications on any machine can compose directly with applications on any other machine.

### Where the "RPC" name comes from

LingoFuse grew out of ZNetV2 — an industrial-grade communication engine with real single-day PB-scale traffic. ZNetV2 is strong at large-scale server-side data throughput, but weak at multi-language collaboration: its interface is Pascal-native, and any other language had to write glue code. In the AI era a single language is no longer sufficient, so LingoFuse broke out: it keeps ZNetV2's kernel (C4 mesh, dual-tunnel, StableIO, HPC thread pool, command bridge, handle pool, soft synchronization, zero-copy mapping) but exposes the whole system through a C ABI that behaves like RPC — request/response, one-way notify, sequenced calls, async callbacks — and it also supports IPC (same-machine shared memory) under the same API surface. We use "RPC" as the unified term for LingoFuse because it has RPC's abstractions, RPC's service discovery and load balancing, and it also eats IPC and multi-language collaboration. ZNetV2 is the technical root; RPC is the public abstraction; multi-language is the user surface. The three together are LingoFuse.

### All languages are equal — no Pascal privilege

Pascal is the implementation language of the core engine, but it is not a privileged language. All 18 first-party bindings go through the same C ABI, the same UTF-8 + NUL wire format, the same little-endian integers, the same compact JSON without `\uXXXX`, the same Handle ownership rules (sync family owned by caller, async family owned by framework), the same side-data semantics (UID / P2PName injected by the sender, read only from the callback's `input` handle), the same test independence, and the same code-generator treatment. There is no "native-language priority" concept anywhere in the binding layer. Pascal can do what Python can do, and vice versa. Team strategy documents that mention "Pascal backend form" or "Pascal reduced to toolchain" are describing team-role division, not language status.

## Stability first, concurrency secondary

LingoFuse places application stability as the top priority; concurrency performance is deliberately deprioritized. This is not a temporary trade-off but a trend the project will maintain in all future versions. A communication layer that occasionally crashes, drops messages, or deadlocks under high concurrency is useless no matter how low its latency is. Therefore, this project does not include horizontal performance comparisons in the main README. For actual measured data under concurrency and stress, refer to the `test/` directory.

## Core capabilities

- Cross-language function calls without IDL or stub generation
- Sub-1ms same-machine IPC latency (self-reported; verify locally)
- Built-in service discovery, load balancing, and FIFO ordering
- Streaming RPC support (Notify)
- Automatic reconnection
- Zero-copy data transfer
- HTTP bridge for browser / Node.js / PHP integration
- PHP integration via HTTP bridge (JSON over HTTP POST, PHP as caller only)
- Deterministic code generation via LingoFuse-Tools
- AI-ready knowledge base system for interface takeover
- C4 service mesh for multi-node discovery and cross-node routing
- P2P load balancing with Cycle_Anchor + Fixed_Sequenced stickiness
- Sequenced families for per-(App, API) and per-(UID, API) FIFO
- Binary handles for video frames / audio chunks / matrices / tensors
- Mesh-join via `password` (same `password` → same mesh; different `password` → physically isolated meshes)

| C++ | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 82 + stress + concurrent | Native C ABI, zero overhead; local test programs under `cpp/test/`, `cpp/Stress/`, `cpp/Conc/` |
| C# / .NET | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | ~60 in `csharp/test/` + `csharp/test2/` suite | Self-built TestCase/TestRunner (no xUnit); P/Invoke + RAII + unified JSON I/O + `CallbackDispatcher` + callback-style async |
| TypeScript | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 223 tests | Complete type definitions; Node / Deno / Bun support |
| JavaScript | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 223 tests | CommonJS + ESM dual entry; byte-level interop with TS |
| Rust | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 174 tests | Safe RAII wrappers + full C ABI layer; `catch_unwind` at FFI boundary |
| Go | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 18 tests | purego (no cgo), cross-compile friendly; e2e / ABI smoke / data handle tests |
| Dart | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | Full test suite | Dart FFI + C bridge DLL; full caller + server capability; Flutter mobile support |
| Java | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 145 tests | FFM API (JDK 22+), pure Java no JNI; `ArenaReaper` for timeout stub; performance optimization ongoing |
| Swift | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 261 XCTest | Clang importer + C target; RAII handles; unified JSON I/O; C++ ↔ Swift bidirectional byte-level interop verified; Windows verified, macOS / Linux untested |
| Zig | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | ~50 `test` blocks + 170+ smoke assertions | Hand-written extern declarations; RAII handles; unified JSON I/O; byte-level compatible with C++ / C# / Rust / Go / Python / JavaScript; locks Zig 0.17.0; Windows x64 verified, Linux / macOS / 32-bit untested |
| Erlang | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 4 EUnit suites | NIF-based; C ABI functions wrapped in RAII-style resources; `lingofuse_json` enforces wire-format contract; async `register_call/4` and sync `register_call_sync/4` callback modes; cross-platform NIF build via `c_src/build.escript`; OTP 27+ with zero third-party runtime deps; Windows verified, Linux / macOS untested |
| Ruby | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 331 tests, 14 files | Fiddle bindings + native C extension for thread-safe callbacks; RAII `DataHandle` / `AppHandle`; unified `LfIo` JSON/string I/O; `NetworkEventQueue` for queue-based event consumption; Windows x64 verified, Linux / macOS untested |
| Fortran | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 474 assertions | Three-layer design: Fortran 2008 `iso_c_binding` → C ABI bridge (`lf_fortran.h` / `lf_fortran.cpp`) → LingoFuse C++ RAII layer; RAII data/app handles; unified JSON/string/byte I/O; native `bind(C)` callbacks via `c_funloc`; allocation-managed string reads; Windows x64 verified, Linux / macOS untested |
| Julia | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 431 + 4 scenarios | C shim (`lf_shim_real.dll`) bridges callbacks from native C4 worker threads into a dedicated Julia consumer thread via a mutex + condvar event queue; blocking calls routed through `@threadcall` to avoid Julia GC safepoint deadlock; RAII `DataHandle` / `App`; unified `io.jl` / `binio.jl` JSON + little-endian binary I/O; `NetworkEventQueue` with bounded queue backpressure; requires `--threads=2`; Windows x64 verified, Linux / macOS / Apple Silicon untested |
| R | Production-ready | ✅ | ✅ | 211 + 5-step chain | Four-layer architecture (R package → C shim → C++ bridge → runtime); Job queue + mutex/condvar bridges single-threaded R interpreter with C4 worker threads; RAII handles via `externalptr` + finalizer; string and binary payload modes; zero-copy `raw` ↔ `std::string`; `lf_local_call` bypasses C4 network for single-process self-tests; no runtime package dependencies; Windows x64 verified (R 4.6.1 + Rtools45), Linux / macOS untested |
| PHP | Caller-only | ❌ | ✅ | No FFI tests | Via `bridge.py` HTTP gateway, JSON over HTTP POST. PHP cannot be a server. Official PHP FFI cannot support C ABI callbacks. |

> Java note: Requires JDK 22+ (JDK 25 LTS recommended). Functionally complete, including cross-process RPC, cross-language ABI verification, and three-process Demo. Performance optimization is still in progress. No GitHub-hosted CI; Java tests run locally via `java/run_test_ci.ps1` / `run_test_ci.sh`.

> Swift note: Requires Swift 5.9+ (6.4 recommended). 261 XCTest cases cover all layers from C ABI to high-level wrappers. Cross-language Demo has verified byte-level bidirectional interop with C++ (integers, strings, floats). Windows fully verified; macOS / Linux C wrapper includes all three platform branches but is not yet tested.

> Zig note: Requires Zig 0.17.0 (that version introduced several breaking API changes). ~50 `test` blocks plus 170+ smoke assertions cover six layers: Zig native unit, C ABI integration, unified I/O, JSON engine, network events, and status queue. Cross-language Demo has verified byte-level compatibility with C++ / C# / Rust / Go / Python / JavaScript. Windows x64 fully verified; Linux / macOS / Windows 32-bit not yet verified.

> Erlang note: Requires Erlang/OTP 27+ (verified on OTP 29). NIF-based binding; C ABI functions available with RAII-style resource types. Unified JSON I/O is enforced through `lingofuse_json` module. Two Call callback modes: `register_call/4` (async, delivers `{lf_call, Api, Payload}`) and `register_call_sync/4` (blocks native caller until `reply/2`). NIF built via `c_src/build.escript` on Windows / Linux / macOS / BSD, auto-selecting available C compiler (gcc / clang / cc / MSVC cl). Zero third-party runtime dependencies — uses OTP 27+ built-in `json` module. Windows verified; Linux / macOS untested.

> Ruby note: Requires Ruby 4.0+ (x64-mingw-ucrt build) with DevKit. Uses `Fiddle` for the C ABI layer plus a small native C extension (`lingofuse_ext.so`) that bridges callbacks from native worker threads into a dedicated Ruby scheduler thread, avoiding the `[BUG] rb_thread_call_with_gvl()` deadlock that pure Fiddle would hit. 331 minitest cases across 14 files; no GitHub-hosted CI, run locally via `ruby/run_test_ci.ps1` (Windows) or `ruby/run_test_ci.sh` (Linux / macOS). Windows x64 fully verified; Linux / macOS not yet tested.

> Fortran note: Requires a Fortran 2008 compiler (`gfortran` recommended), a C++17 compiler, a C11 compiler, and GNU Make. The C++ compiler and Fortran compiler must come from the same toolchain distribution — otherwise linking fails with `undefined reference to __gfortran_*`. The binding uses a three-layer design: Fortran 2008 (`iso_c_binding` + `bind(C)`) → C ABI bridge (`lf_fortran.h` / `lf_fortran.cpp`, exporting `extern "C"` symbols, absorbing exceptions, encoding UTF-8) → LingoFuse C++ RAII layer (`LingoFuse.hpp` / `lf_io.hpp`). 474 assertions across 3 suites: C ABI tests, Fortran binding tests, and Fortran JSON tests. Cross-language Demo validates byte-level interop against C++ (`cross_call_cpp.exe`). Windows x64 verified; Linux / macOS not yet tested.

> Julia note: Requires Julia 1.9+ (1.13.1 verified) and must be launched with `--threads=2` or higher — the callback consumer task cannot run on the main thread, and the binding raises `LingoFuseStateError` at startup otherwise. Because Julia's GC, JIT, and Task scheduler all require threads to be adopted by the runtime, callbacks from C4 worker threads cannot enter Julia directly; a small pure-native C shim (`lf_shim_real.dll` / `.so` / `.dylib`) snapshots each event into a queue and blocks the C4 worker until a dedicated Julia consumer thread finishes handling it. Any C call that may block (`LF_Call`, `LF_PrepareDone`, `LF_ExitMainThread`, `LF_Shutdown`, `LF_LocalCall`, `LF_LocalNotify`, `LF_Notify`, `LF_Sequenced_Notify`) is dispatched via `@threadcall` on libuv's thread pool to keep the calling Julia thread at a GC safepoint. 431 assertions + 4 scenarios across 8 test files, all passing. Uses JSON3.jl (the only external dependency). Windows x64 verified; Linux / macOS / Apple Silicon not yet tested. `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` (default 4) constrains `@threadcall` concurrency for Cross Demo load tests.

> R note: Requires R 4.0+ (verified on R 4.6.1 ucrt x64) and, on Windows, Rtools45 for compiling the bridge layer. Because the R interpreter is single-threaded, callbacks from C4 worker threads cannot enter R directly; a pure-native C++ shim (`lfR_bridge.dll`) snapshots each event into a Job queue (with atomic refcounts and per-event timeout) and blocks the C4 worker until the R main thread picks it up from a user-driven pump loop (`lf_poll`). The binding uses a four-layer architecture (R package → C shim with `R.h` → C++ bridge with no R headers → LingoFuse runtime), because R 4.6's `R.h` relies on C11 anonymous unions that MSVC cannot compile. Two payload modes: string mode (default; UTF-8 + NUL stripping) and binary mode (`bin=TRUE`; raw bytes preserved). RAII handles are managed via R `externalptr` + `CFinalizer`, so GC collects them safely. `LF_Call` is not reentrant — single-process self-tests must use `lf_local_call` / `lf_local_notify`, which dispatch directly through the R handler table without touching C4. The R package has zero runtime dependencies (no `jsonlite` in `Imports`). 211 assertions + 5-step chain; the C++ test binaries are built alongside the shim. `R CMD check` passes with `Status: OK`. Cannot be submitted to CRAN — the runtime is an external binary dependency. Windows x64 verified; Linux / macOS untested.

> PHP note: PHP can only act as a caller. If you need PHP as a server, LingoFuse currently does not satisfy that requirement.

### Via code generator / bridge

| Language / Platform | Method | Maturity |
|---|---|---|
| Node.js / Browser | `bridge.py` HTTP gateway | Usable, non-native |
| Kotlin / Lua / Elixir / Nim / Crystal | Via LingoFuse-Tools code generator | Generated code usable, requires own verification |
| aarch64 / loongarch64 / RISC-V | Edge device porting planned | In progress, not production-ready |

> Swift, Zig, Erlang, Ruby, Fortran, Julia, and R were previously listed under code-generator / bridge integration. All seven have been promoted to first-party bindings and are no longer accessed via the code generator.

## Cross-language interop (Cross Demo)

LingoFuse's core promise is "functions written in any language can be called directly from any other language." To validate this, every first-party binding ships with a set of three Cross programs sharing the same wire-format contract.

### Three-process roles

| Program | Role | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `CrossService` | Coordinator (beacon) | Creates IPC endpoint `ipc:cross`; registers no APIs |
| `CrossNode` | Worker node | Registers `demo` app with two APIs: `add` and `inv_seri` |
| `CrossCall` | Load-test client | 32 threads × 10 seconds against the `demo` app |

### Shared wire-format contract

```
add       (int32 a, int32 b)                       -> int32
inv_seri  (uint8, uint16, uint32, uint64,
           string(NUL), float)                     -> reversed types
```

String = UTF-8 + NUL; integers = little-endian; floats = IEEE 754 little-endian. Any language's `CrossCall` that correctly reads bytes written by another language's `CrossNode` proves 100% multi-language interop for those two languages. This is empirical validation, not theoretical inference.

### Cross Demo locations per language

| Language | Location |
|---|---|
| Pascal | `pascal/cross_demo/` |
| C++ | `cpp/CrossDemo/` |
| C# | `csharp/CrossService/`, `csharp/CrossNode/`, `csharp/CrossCall/` |
| Swift | `swift/Sources/CrossService/`, `swift/Sources/CrossNode/`, `swift/Sources/CrossCall/` |
| Zig | `zig/examples/` (`cross_service.zig`, `cross_node.zig`, `cross_call.zig`) |
| Erlang | `erlang/cross/` (`cross_service.escript`, `cross_node.escript`, `cross_call.escript`) |
| Ruby | `ruby/cross/` (`cross_service.rb`, `cross_node.rb`, `cross_call.rb`) |
| Fortran | `fortran/cross_demo/` (`cross_service.f90`, `cross_node.f90`, `cross_call.f90`, `cross_call_cpp.cpp`) |
| Julia | `julia/example/` (`CrossService.jl`, `CrossNode.jl`, `CrossCall.jl`) |
| R | `r/c_ext/tests/cross_node.R` (paired with `cross_client.cpp`) |
| Rust | `rust/examples/` |
| Go | `go/cross/` |
| TypeScript | `ts/cross/` |
| JavaScript | `js/cross/` |
| Python | `Py/cross/` |
| Java | `java/src/main/java/lingofuse/demo/cross/` |

### Verified interop directions

| Direction | Result |
|---|---|
| Swift ↔ C++ | ✅ Verified |
| Zig ↔ C++ / C# / Rust / Go / Python / JavaScript | ✅ Byte-level compatible |
| Erlang ↔ C++ / C# / Python / JavaScript | ✅ Byte-level interoperable |
| Ruby ↔ C++ / C# / Python / JavaScript | ✅ Byte-level compatible (shared wire-format contract; validated by test suite) |
| Fortran ↔ C++ | ✅ Verified (Fortran `CrossNode` served both Fortran `CrossCall` and C++ `cross_call_cpp` with identical bytes) |
| Julia ↔ C++ / C# / Pascal / Python / JavaScript | ✅ Byte-level compatible (shared wire-format contract; validated by test suite) |
| R ↔ C++ | ✅ Verified (R `cross_node.R` served the C++ `cross_client.exe` for both `demo.add` and `demo.inv_seri` raw binary APIs) |
| Pascal ↔ C++ | ✅ Verified |
| C# ↔ C++ | ✅ Verified |
| Rust ↔ C++ | ✅ Verified |

## Quick start

```bash
git clone --recursive https://github.com/PassByYou888/LingoFuse.git
cd LingoFuse
```

Then read the test guides under `test/` and run the pre-compiled executables inside `test/test.zip`. You get real data from your own hardware.

For deeper verification, compile the C++ test programs yourself:

```bash
cd cpp/test   && cmake . && make && ./test_lingofuse
cd cpp/Stress && cmake . && make && ./StressService & ./StressClient
cd cpp/Conc   && cmake . && make && ./ConcService  & ./ConcClient
```

## Building the dynamic library

`src/` is the entry point for building the LingoFuse core dynamic library. Prepare a Pascal compilation environment (FPC / Lazarus), then one-click build.

| Document | Content |
|---|---|
| `src/CONTRIBUTING.md` | Build environment setup and workflow |
| `src/CONTRIBUTING_lazbuild.md` | One-click build with lazbuild CLI; includes LoongArch64 manual Lazarus build steps |
| `src/FPC_3.3.1_Package_Info.md` | FPC 3.3.1 environment package info |
| `src/Lazarus_Change_FPC.md` | Switching FPC version in Lazarus |

### Core build files

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `src/build.bat` | Windows one-click build script |
| `src/LingoFuse.lpi` | Lazarus project file |
| `src/LingoFuse.lpr` | Project main program file |
| `src/Z.LingoFuse_Core.pas` | Core engine implementation |
| `src/Z.LingoFuse_Export.pas` | C ABI export layer |

One-click build:

```bash
cd src
lazbuild LingoFuse.lpi
```

Note: FPC toolchain has version lock-in — all build machines must use the same FPC 3.3.1 build source, otherwise `PPU version mismatch` will occur. See `src/CONTRIBUTING.md`. The current include paths in `src/*.pas` use Windows-style backslashes; FPC on Linux / macOS does not resolve them, so building on those platforms requires editing the scripts first. Cross-platform support is therefore: Windows verified; Linux / macOS need user-side verification.

## Testing & verification: `test/` is the source of truth

For any uncertainty about the README — latency, ordering, stability, behavior under concurrency — do not guess. Go to `test/` and find physical verification.

### What `test/` provides

`test/` provides part of the PoC (Proof of Concept) work. Before using LingoFuse in production, note:

1. The author provides race-condition stability tests (the most important mechanism-level tests), but not your App-level tests. You need to simulate your own App layer and run a PoC to verify LF's behavior in your specific business scenario.
2. You need to be able to build and compile LF yourself. LingoFuse is developed by Lao Zhang; if it is not maintained long-term, users need to build it themselves and keep up with generational updates.
3. Each language has its own test / CI system in principle. All 18 languages ship runnable local tests; the root repository has no GitHub-hosted CI, and the only workflow in the tree is `erlang/.github/workflows/ci.yml`:
   - C++: `cpp/test/`, `cpp/Stress/`, `cpp/Conc/`
   - Java: `java/run_test_ci.ps1`, `java/run_test_ci.sh`
   - Swift: `swift/test.ps1`, `swift/Tests/LingoFuseTests/`
   - Zig: `zig/test.ps1`, `zig/tests/`, `zig/examples/`
   - Erlang: `erlang/test.ps1`, `erlang/test/`
   - Ruby: `ruby/run_test_ci.ps1`, `ruby/run_test_ci.sh`, `ruby/test/`
   - Fortran: `fortran/test.ps1`, `fortran/build.ps1`, `fortran/check_env.ps1`, `fortran/c_ext/`
   - Julia: `julia/test.ps1`, `julia/test/runtests.jl`, `julia/check_env.ps1`
   - R: `r/c_ext/tests/` (five-step chain), plus `r/check_env.ps1`, `r/build.ps1`, `r/test.ps1`
   - Go: `go/test.ps1`, `go/dev_test.ps1`
   - Rust: `rust/test.ps1`
   - C#: `csharp/build.ps1`, `csharp/test/`, `csharp/test2/`
   - TypeScript: `ts/package.json`, `ts/test/`
   - Python: `Py/lingofuse/test_lingofuse.py`, `Py/lingofuse/test_bridge.py`
   - JavaScript: `js/test/test.js`
   - Dart: `dart/test/`
   - Pascal: various Demo and test projects under `pascal/`

### Why `test/` contains documents and executables instead of GitHub Actions

GitHub's automated CI has many limitations. LingoFuse supports multiple languages and platforms — Pascal, Python, C++, C#, TypeScript, JavaScript, Rust, Go, Dart, Java, Swift, Zig, Erlang, Ruby, Fortran, Julia, R, PHP, across Windows / Linux / macOS, covering IPC / TCP / cross-machine deployment forms. Putting all combinations into GitHub's hosted runners is neither convenient nor realistic.

So LingoFuse's approach is: deliver testing capability directly to the user. `test/` provides complete test guides (Markdown) and pre-compiled executables (`test/test.zip`). You extract, run, and observe on your own machine — getting real data from your own hardware.

The root repository currently hosts no GitHub Actions workflow. The only workflow in the tree is `erlang/.github/workflows/ci.yml`. Everything else is a runnable local test program. C++ test source code (the largest suite) lives under `cpp/`:

- `cpp/test/` — Functional tests (`test_lingofuse.cpp` / `test_lingofuse_json.cpp`)
- `cpp/Stress/` — Stress tests (`StressService.cpp` / `StressClient.cpp` / `StressMonitor.cpp`)
- `cpp/Conc/` — Concurrent Notify tests (`ConcService.cpp` / `ConcClient.cpp`)

Each subdirectory has `CMakeLists.txt` and one-click local scripts.

### Test documents & executables

## Code generator system

LingoFuse-Tools solves the biggest pain point of cross-language RPC: writing bindings for each language by hand.

Give it a Pascal unit or C header file, and it automatically produces multi-language server, client, and companion README documentation.

| Tool | Target | Protocol | Target languages |
|---|---|---|---|
| code_decl_to_abi | ABI server / client | LingoFuse binary ABI | 17 languages (Pascal / Python / C++ / C# / Rust / Go / Java / Node.js / TypeScript / Erlang / Julia / Zig / Swift / Ruby / Fortran / Dart / R) |
| code_decl_to_json_abi | HTTP/JSON server / client | HTTP + JSON (via bridge) | 20+ languages (the 17 above + JavaScript browser + PHP + Delphi + Bridge launcher scripts) |
| code_decl_to_mcp | MCP tool provider | Model Context Protocol | Pascal / Python / C++ / C# |

Each tool has three entry points: GUI, CLI, and MCP API. Each tool comes with a self-contained knowledge base (Markdown) covering API contracts, wire protocol, type mapping, known pitfalls, debugging trees, and extension guides.

Feed the knowledge base to an AI, and the AI can assist in taking over the interface — generated code still requires human verification. The knowledge base and MCP API are generated from the same source, so they never diverge.

See: https://github.com/PassByYou888/LingoFuse-Tools

## Ecosystem projects built on LingoFuse

LingoFuse is a communication foundation. The foundation itself does not build applications, but many kinds of buildings can be built on top of it.

### Agent runtimes

| Project | Language | Status | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| pasAgent v2 | Pascal | Released | Text agent, 129+ LLM backends |
| pasAgent v3 | Pascal | Released | Multimodal agent, 250+ backends, dual-language code generation |
| cppAgent | C++ | Released | C++ ecosystem agent integration |
| csharpAgent | C# / .NET | Released | .NET agent runtime + LLM client SDK |
| tsAgent | TypeScript | Coming soon | TypeScript / JavaScript ecosystem agent runtime |

> tsAgent is not yet released. The current TS/JS bindings are pure communication layers, without an agent runtime. If you need to build agents in TS/JS, use mature frameworks like Mastra or Vercel AI SDK, then call functions in other languages through LingoFuse's TS bindings.

These branches demonstrate that the LingoFuse communication foundation is general enough to support agent layers built in any language ecosystem — and the foundation ensures they can talk to each other.

### Related projects

- zIPC — The same-machine IPC engine under LingoFuse. Use zIPC directly if you only need same-machine IPC without the full RPC mesh.
- ZNetV2 — The large-scale server-side data throughput framework in the PassByYou888 stack; the technical root of LingoFuse.
- LingoFuse-Tools — The code generator system.

## Dependencies

Core dynamic libraries are located in `Binary/`:

| Platform | Core library | IPC dependency | Memory allocator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows 64 | `LingoFuse64.dll` | `z_ipc_64.dll` | `mimalloc64.dll` |
| Windows 32 | `LingoFuse32.dll` | `z_ipc_32.dll` | `mimalloc32.dll` |
| Linux | `liblingofuse.so` | `libz_ipc.so` | `libmimalloc.so` (optional) |
| macOS | `liblingofuse.dylib` | `libz_ipc.dylib` | `libmimalloc.dylib` (optional) |

> The current `Binary/` directory mainly provides Windows 32/64-bit pre-compiled libraries. Linux / macOS libraries must be compiled according to the build documents under `src/`.

Deployment: Add the `Binary/` directory to system `PATH`, or copy the dynamic libraries to the executable's directory.

On Windows, install the VC++ 2015-2022 Redistributable:
- Download page: Latest supported Visual C++ Redistributable downloads
- x64 direct link: https://aka.ms/vs/17/release/vc_redist.x64.exe
- x86 direct link: https://aka.ms/vs/17/release/vc_redist.x86.exe

## Network join and password

LingoFuse is a mesh, not a set of freely connectable sockets. Every process that wants to interoperate must join the mesh first. The join credential is the `password` option, set via `LF_SetOption("password", "...")` or each language's typed setter. This applies to both IPC (same-machine shared memory) and TCP (cross-machine) — IPC is not a bypass.

- `get_option("password")` always returns `'********'`, never the real value.
- Different passwords place processes in physically isolated meshes: they cannot see, route to, or call each other. This is by design, not a bug.
- IPC is unencrypted (data never leaves the host). TCP uses symmetric encryption by default (`SwitchDefaultPerformance` tier, 15 selectable ciphers including DES / Blowfish legacy algorithms), but the default tier does not enable frame integrity checking (`hsNone`). For tamper resistance, either pick a higher tier or add application-layer integrity checks.
- The default password must be changed in production. The default `'DTC40@ZSERVER'` is shared by every unconfigured LF process, which is convenient for development and dangerous in production.

See `doc/LF_Network_Join.md` for the full network-join contract and the list of facts that are still not fully documented (exact failure behavior, multi-server consistency rules, password length/charset constraints).

## Not recommended for

- Projects requiring mature community support, extensive third-party tutorials, or Stack Overflow Q&A.
- Teams that cannot accept single-maintainer risk and lack the ability to compile and maintain LF themselves.
- Pure TS/JS projects where all logic can be rewritten in TS/JS — introducing LF only adds complexity and failure points.
- Scenarios requiring PHP as a server (PHP can only be a caller).
- Teams with hard concurrency performance requirements who are unwilling to run their own App-level PoC verification.
- Flutter Web projects (Dart FFI unavailable).
- 32-bit Windows projects (Dart binding untested).
- Java binding requires JDK 22+; cannot run directly on JDK 8 / 11 / 17 / 21.
- Swift binding requires Swift 5.9+ (6.4 recommended); macOS / Linux deployment paths not yet tested.
- Zig binding locks Zig 0.17.0; before upgrading to 0.18+ the breaking API change list must be re-evaluated. Linux / macOS / 32-bit platforms not yet verified.
- Erlang binding requires Erlang/OTP 27+; NIF crashes take down the BEAM node; never call blocking LingoFuse functions from callbacks.
- Ruby binding requires Ruby 4.0+ (x64-mingw-ucrt) with DevKit for the native C extension; Linux / macOS not yet tested; no GitHub-hosted CI.
- Fortran binding requires Fortran 2008 + C++17 + C11 toolchain, and the C++ / Fortran compilers must come from the same distribution; Linux / macOS theoretically supported but untested.
- Julia binding must be launched with `--threads=2` or higher — the callback consumer cannot run on the main thread and the binding raises `LingoFuseStateError` otherwise. `@threadcall` concurrency is bounded by libuv's thread pool (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, default 4). Linux / macOS / Apple Silicon not yet tested; no GitHub-hosted CI.
- R binding requires R 4.0+ and, on Windows, Rtools45. `LF_Call` is not reentrant — single-process self-tests must use `lf_local_call` / `lf_local_notify`. The R package cannot be submitted to CRAN because the runtime is an external binary dependency. Linux / macOS not yet tested; no GitHub-hosted CI.

## Documentation map

### Top-level entry points

- README: Main entry, read-by-role guide
- llms.txt: LLM-optimized summary (this file)

- LF-Architecture-Unreplicable-Backend-Systems.md: Why an equivalent LF is not economically replicable even with full source and docs (implicit contract density, AI's architecture-boundary)
- LingoFuse_MultiLanguage_Complete_Guide.md: Authoritative multi-language reference (v2.0)
- LingoFuse_MultiLanguage_Deployment_Guide_v3.0.md: Per-language deployment guide (v3.0)
- LingoFuse_P2P_Distributed_Load_Concept.md: P2P and distributed load concept
